reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes The Fortune Miner through unusually high BNB return claims, including 3% daily in the title, up to 11% daily in the narration, and a displayed 3.33% daily and 1215.45% APR offer, while presenting a personal deposit and reported earnings as part of the promotion. The participation flow requires depositing BNB and using repeated compounding, withdrawals, and redeposits, includes a stated 90% tax for claiming without compounding, and connects the system's operation with recruiting additional players. Although the speaker gives high-risk and no-guarantee disclaimers, the discussion describes the project as initially operating as a Ponzi and continues to present referral and participation incentives tied to the miner.

opening.argument: Judge the return figures as investment commentary about a risky, variable protocol, not a promise of income. The speaker says the yield will change, calls participation a high-risk game, and tells viewers to research it rather than follow his lead. He even states that the project will start as a Ponzi while its proposed revenue sources develop. That admission is difficult to square with an attempt to conceal the central risk. The description likewise says earnings are not guaranteed. These warnings do not make the investment sound, but they matter when deciding whether the video deceptively assures viewers of a return.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats an advertised maximum and a personal dashboard figure as if they were assured future payments. But the speaker explicitly calls his current yield variable and says it will change. Nor does identifying a deposit and compounding rule establish that he hid the downside: he warns that simply claiming without compounding incurs a 90% tax. The cited offer is aggressive, but the narration supplies material limits a viewer would need to weigh it.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Warnings do not undo the video's affirmative sales pitch. The speaker reports earning more than 11% daily, gives a repeatable compound-and-withdraw strategy, and calls it the “secret sauce for beating miners.” Most importantly, his Ponzi admission concerns this project's beginning, not merely an abstract risk. The defense's quotes show that he disclosed dangers; they do not make the promoted return mechanism ordinary investment commentary.

opening.argument: The video does more than display a headline yield: it walks through how the miner calculates a participant's share and why claiming without hiring more miners can reduce daily earnings. It explains the 90% withdrawal tax condition and the limit on how long rewards accumulate without action. The speaker also describes the result as a game against other participants, dependent on TVL and their behavior. A careful judge can read this as an operational demonstration that exposes consequential mechanics, including unfavorable ones, rather than a simple instruction to trust a return figure.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies deposits and repeated transactions, but those facts also explain why a walkthrough would cover compounding, claiming and redepositing. Its dashboard example is the speaker's stated personal position, not evidence that every viewer would get the same result. He explicitly distinguishes the illustrated current yield from a stable rate. The mechanics are troubling; the opening has not shown that explaining them is itself a false demonstration.

opening.argument: This is a review of a named crypto product with disclosed participation terms, not evidence of a completed fraud. The speaker specifies a minimum and maximum BNB deposit, describes a 1% referral bonus, and says he will link the project's documentation for viewers to inspect. The description also discloses that some links may earn him a commission. Depositing BNB is plainly part of the product, but the supplied material does not show a guaranteed payout, a request for credentials, or an actual loss or failed withdrawal. A referral feature and a high advertised rate warrant scrutiny; neither alone proves that this particular presentation deceived viewers.

rebuttal.rebuttal: A dashboard deposit and an advertised daily rate show what the product asks users to do and what it claims, but not that the displayed earnings were paid out or that viewers were guaranteed the same return. The opening's recruitment point also needs precision: the narration mentions a 1% referral bonus, while the description discloses possible affiliate commissions. Those are incentives to examine, not by themselves proof of a hidden downline or a realized loss.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A realized loss or credential request is not necessary to evaluate the promotion. The speaker describes depositing BNB for miners that earn a share of the contract, promotes daily BNB returns, and acknowledges that this project starts as a Ponzi. The missing proof of a failed withdrawal does not turn the deposit-and-return pitch into ordinary commerce; the referral bonus is an additional incentive, not the core concern.
